title: Whom Does AI Serve? Whom Do We?
author: Gary Houchens
summary: Education writer Gary Houchens summarizes and endorses a recent speech by artist and podcaster Jonathan Pageau, which uses the Arthurian legend of the Holy Grail -- and the knights' obligation to ask 'whom does the Grail serve?' -- as a symbol for the question Pageau argues society must relentlessly ask of AI and modern technology more broadly. Building on Paul Kingsnorth's concept of 'the Machine' (the global techno-economic system Kingsnorth argues has materially enriched humanity while spiritually and socially damaging it), Pageau's argument, as relayed here, is that since AI's advance is unstoppable, the only remaining point of leverage is personal: becoming 'more human than before' so as to remain master of the Machine rather than its slave. The piece's central educational claim is that classical, liberal-arts education -- music, dance, sport, memory, virtue -- is not a nostalgic alternative to technological competence but the direct answer to AI's threat, because these practices deliberately cultivate the internal human faculties (memory, skill, knowledge, 'singing souls') that AI otherwise pushes people to outsource and lose. Houchens closes by explicitly linking this argument to his own broader conviction that a return to traditional religious belief and classical education represents the most promising path toward a thriving human future in an AI-saturated world.
points: The Holy Grail framing gives the essay's central question a memorable, transferable form: 'whom does this technology serve?' is presented as the same obligatory diagnostic question the Arthurian knights failed to ask, with the same consequence (great suffering) for institutions and individuals who fail to ask it of AI.

The essay's practical answer to an otherwise unstoppable technological force is explicitly personal and formational rather than political or regulatory: becoming 'more human than before' through deliberately cultivated memory, skill, and virtue is presented as the only leverage point left once AI's advance itself cannot be halted.

Classical, liberal-arts practices (music, dance, sport) are reframed as direct countermeasures to a specific mechanism of AI harm -- AI pushes memory, skill, and knowledge 'out there' into external systems, so education must deliberately foster the same capacities 'in here,' inside the person, as a counterbalance.

The piece treats classical education's traditional aims -- virtue, wisdom, 'ordered love' -- as its actual purpose rather than incidental byproducts, explicitly arguing these are the qualities that determine who 'will survive and thrive' as AI's influence deepens, not merely nice-to-have enrichments.
quotes: The Machine" is Kingsnorth's metaphor for the global techno-economic system that has brought an unprecedented quality of material life to humankind but has nearly destroyed us spiritually, psychologically, and socially. Artificial intelligence is perhaps the most vivid and powerful manifestation of the Machine.

Pageau, speaking to the Alliance for Responsible Citizenship conference in London recently, challenged his audience to be relentless in asking the questions, "Whom does AI serve? And whom do we serve?

If we cannot stop the machine from devouring everything then you, then I, must become truly human. More human than before. So that we can remain, at least in our life, the master of the machine and not the slave of the machine.

I say back to the humanities. Those will become the more important. Make humans become fully human. And when we teach our children to dance or play music or play sports … we teach them these skills so they become more human. If AI pushes us to place memory and skill and knowledge out there, we will have to deliberately foster memory and skill and knowledge in here…

I really believe that it's only those who have singing souls, who have fostered wisdom and virtue, who have practiced truth and love, they are the ones who will survive and thrive in the incoming AI apocalypse.
Singing souls, practiced virtue, and ordered love aren't incidental benefits of classical education. They are its purpose.
